passage: Rain drummed on the wedding tent, and drips fell on the last row of plastic chairs. Ujjwal, ten, watched the relatives crowd around his uncle, the bank manager, who was given the front seat under the dry part and a garland. Ujjwal's father, who drove a delivery van, stood at the back by the food counter with a folded newspaper over his head. Nobody called him forward. Ujjwal's stomach felt heavy. Afreen Aunty from next door handed him a napkin. "My father stitched shirts in a tiny shop. Best hands in the lane. Work is only small when it is done carelessly." Ujjwal looked at his father's dripping sleeves, then walked over and held the newspaper higher.

qa.q: Where was Ujjwal's father standing at the wedding?
qa.a: He stood at the back by the food counter.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling when he watched the relatives around his uncle?
qa.a: He felt sad and a little ashamed, shown by his heavy stomach as his father stood unnoticed at the back.

qa.q: What choices did Afreen Aunty and Ujjwal make that showed dignity in every kind of work?
qa.a: Afreen Aunty spoke proudly of her father's skilled hands at stitching, and Ujjwal walked over to hold the newspaper higher for his father.

qa.q: What might it be like for Ujjwal's father, standing at the back in the rain?
qa.a: He may feel overlooked while relatives crowd the uncle, although the passage does not say what he thinks, and he may be glad to have Ujjwal come to his side.

grounding: A child sees relatives treat a parent with a senior post differently from one in a small job, and an adult teaches that honest work carries dignity.

passage:
After Chacha's housewarming, Saurabh, nine, sat on the stairs with his sketchbook. All evening the relatives had called his uncle "Sir", asked about his promotion and fussed over his tea. When Saurabh's father came in, still in his guard's uniform from the night shift, only two people said hello. Saurabh drew nothing.
At home Mummy asked, "What's wrong?"
"Everybody likes Chacha's job more."
Madhuri sat on the step beside him. "Every night your father opens the gate for two hundred families and knows each child by name. Ask him tomorrow who forgot their keys."
Next morning Saurabh asked. His father laughed and listed six names, each with a story.

qa.q: Who did the relatives call 'Sir' at the housewarming?
qa.a: They called Saurabh's uncle 'Sir'.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling as he sat on the stairs without drawing?
qa.a: He felt hurt and let down on his father's behalf, shown by 'Everybody likes Chacha's job more.'

qa.q: What did Madhuri do that helped Saurabh see his father's work differently?
qa.a: She told him what his father does each night and sent him to ask about the families, so the job became people and stories instead of a lower rank.

qa.q: How might Saurabh's father have felt when only two people greeted him at the housewarming?
qa.a: He may have felt tired and overlooked after the night shift, though he laughed and told stories readily when Saurabh asked about his work.

grounding: A child sees relatives treat a parent in a small job differently, and an adult teaches that honest work of any kind carries dignity.

passage:
"Mummy, why did everyone stand up when Mama came in?"
"He's a senior officer, Pradeep. People respect his post."
"But when Papa came in, nobody stood up. Bua didn't even give him a chair."
Indu was quiet. "Papa drives a bus. Some people think that's a small job."
"Is it small?"
"What do you think? Who takes a hundred people to work every morning?"
"...Papa."
"And who brought Dadi to the hospital at midnight, in the rain?"
"Papa."
"Then is his job small?"
Pradeep shook his head. "But why do they treat him like that?"
"Because some grown-ups forget that honest work is honest work. Don't you forget it."
Pradeep walked over, pulled out a chair, and put it beside his father.

qa.q: Who brought Dadi to the hospital at midnight?
qa.a: Papa brought Dadi to the hospital at midnight, in the rain.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when he noticed nobody stood for Papa?
qa.a: Pradeep felt confused and a little hurt, noticing that relatives treated his father as less important.

qa.q: How did Indu help Pradeep understand?
qa.a: She asked him questions about what Papa actually does, so he could see for himself that honest work has dignity.

qa.q: How might Papa feel when Pradeep brings him a chair?
qa.a: Papa would probably feel touched and proud, seeing his son respect him in front of the relatives.

grounding: A child notices relatives treat a senior officer better than his bus-driver father, and his mother teaches that honest work carries dignity.

passage:
When I was ten, I noticed something at every family wedding. My uncle, a bank manager, got the best seat. My father, an electrician, fixed the lights and ate last in the kitchen. I'm Himani, his only daughter, and I thought that meant my father was worth less.
Once I told my friend Zeenat, "My uncle is bigger than my papa." Zeenat's father drove an autorickshaw. She looked at me strangely and said, "My abba says there's no small work, only small people."
At the next wedding, the power went out. Everyone panicked. My father fixed it in five minutes, in the dark. The whole hall clapped. My uncle clapped too.
I'm twelve now. I still remember that clapping. And Zeenat's words.

qa.q: What was Himani's father's job?
qa.a: Himani's father was an electrician.

qa.q: How did Himani feel when she watched her father eat last in the kitchen?
qa.a: Himani felt confused and a bit ashamed, thinking it meant her father was worth less.

qa.q: What helped change Himani's view?
qa.a: Zeenat's words about there being no small work, and seeing her father fix the power while everyone clapped, taught her that honest work carries dignity.

qa.q: How might Himani's father have felt when the hall clapped?
qa.a: Her father probably felt proud and appreciated, finally seen for the work he does.

grounding: A child sees relatives treat a manager better than her electrician father and absorbs that work equals rank, until a friend and an event show honest work's dignity.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 4, "My Parent's Job" day.
Children spoke about their parents' work. When Sudha said her mother was a doctor, the class said "Wow!" When Keerthana stood up, she said quietly, "My appa is only a driver," and sat down fast.
I asked her, "Only?" She shrugged. "My aunty says drivers aren't important."
I asked who had come to school by car, bus or van. Almost every hand went up. "Who drove?" Silence, then giggles, then understanding. Sudha said, "My mummy couldn't reach the hospital without a driver."
Keerthana looked up.
I told them that every honest job has dignity, and that "only" is not a word for anyone's work.
Next step: I've asked Keerthana's father to come and talk to the class about his day.

qa.q: What did Keerthana say about her appa?
qa.a: She said quietly, "My appa is only a driver."

qa.q: What does Keerthana sitting down fast suggest she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt embarrassed and ashamed of her father's job after hearing the class praise a doctor.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped the class learn?
qa.a: The teacher showed how everyone depends on drivers, said every honest job has dignity, and invited Keerthana's father to talk to the class.

qa.q: How might Sudha see Keerthana's father's work after the lesson?
qa.a: Sudha seems to understand now that even her doctor mother depends on drivers, and may respect his work more.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child who has absorbed that her father's job is lesser, and a lesson that honest work of any kind carries dignity.

passage:
Joseph's diary, Sunday.
At Grandma's lunch, everyone stood up when Uncle Thomas came in. He is a big officer in the railways. Aunty gave him the chair with the cushion and the first plate of fish. Nobody stood up when Pappa came in. Pappa is a bus conductor. He sat on the steel stool.
Cousin Leela said her dad's job is "more important". I didn't say anything, but my face went hot.
On the bus home I asked Pappa if his job was small. He laughed. "Joseph, who got your Grandma to church every Sunday for ten years? Who gets two hundred people to work every morning?" Then he said, "Every honest job holds something up."
I'm writing that in my school book. Next time I'm giving Pappa the cushion chair.

qa.q: What job does Uncle Thomas have?
qa.a: He is a big officer in the railways.

qa.q: Why did Joseph's face go hot when Leela spoke?
qa.a: Joseph felt embarrassed and hurt for Pappa, sensing that Pappa was being treated as less important.

qa.q: How did Pappa help Joseph see work differently?
qa.a: He answered with a laugh and real examples of the good his work does, and said every honest job holds something up.

qa.q: How might Pappa have felt sitting on the steel stool?
qa.a: Pappa may have noticed the difference and felt a little slighted, but his easy laugh later suggests he is secure in the worth of his work.

grounding: It illustrates a child who sees relatives treat a senior official better than a parent in a small job, and a parent who teaches that honest work carries dignity.
